claims.text: **What happened is solid.** Four Gemini 4 Argon agents went from a random seed to "Free the End" in 27h14m on Java 1.20.4 at Easy difficulty.
They wrote 2,783 programs, died 605 times and needed no human intervention, according to the authors' logs and an Observer agent [^1,2].
According to the authors, "no game strategy was provided" [^2].
The team lit a Nether portal at 1h42m and had 15 ender pearls in a shared chest by 5h30m.
Bringing back blaze powder took more than six hours [^2].
At 10h45m janesick triangulated the stronghold from Eye of Ender throws, landing about 1.3 km away and 43 m off the actual portal room.
The End portal was lit with 12 eyes at 13h17m [^2].
The dragon killed players 69 times, and at 17h30m all four agents jumped into the void within six minutes to force a dragon reset [^2].
All ten fell over the next 4h40m, and the dragon died 39 minutes after the last one, with bulicame at 2.5 of 20 health [^2].
The End portal opened at 13h17m and the win came at 27h14m, so 13h57m, about 51% of the run, was spent in or around the final fight [^2].
The authors call it "our general-purpose Gemini 4 Argon coding agent", and Google DeepMind promoted it from its own account [^2,36].

Google's model page describes Argon as a flagship reasoning model built for "autonomous multi-step agents, and long decode up to 1M tokens", and that is the use case this run was designed to show [^39].
Elsewhere the paper says the agents read that state "down to the number of its current behavior phase" [^2].
`bot.findBlocks` searches the loaded chunks for blocks matching a type within a distance (16 blocks by default, and the caller can raise it).
Visibility is a separate, opt-in `canSeeBlock` raycast [^4,5].
Mineflayer's README advertises "block knowledge… milliseconds to find any block", along with entity tracking, physics, crafting, digging and building [^3].
It offers 13 goal types, from `GoalNear` to `GoalFollow`.
Pathfinding cannot climb ladders or vines, door handling is "unreliable", and the server still enforces melee reach and real-time combat [^6].
Voyager (May 2023) also ran GPT-4 on Mineflayer.
It added 11 hand-written control primitives such as `mineBlock`, `killMob` and `smeltItem`, and it never left the Overworld tech tree [^7,8].
By that standard Argon had less scaffolding: the paper says the pathfinder was loaded with "no helpers added", and the agents built their own 42 helper functions [^2].
METR's own guidance is that measured AI time horizons are "40-100x lower for visual computer use tasks, due to eg poor perception" than for text-native work [^23].
At roughly 22 deaths per wall-clock hour across the team, the strategy was to accept death and retry rather than avoid risk [^2].
A mob that deals D damage on Normal deals min(D, 0.5D+1) on Easy and 1.5D on Hard.
Starvation on Easy stops at 10 HP (five hearts), so hunger alone can never kill a player [^13].
The dragon's melee hit is 6 HP on Easy against 10 on Normal and 15 on Hard, and its wing strike is 3.5 against 5 and 7.5 [^13].
Its breath does 3 HP per second on every difficulty [^13].
A player who dies drops their inventory at the spot, and those drops "decay after five minutes while that chunk is loaded" [^16].
auratian drowned carrying all twelve Eyes of Ender, teammates relayed the exact position and despawn minute, and bulicame recovered them "with two and a half minutes to spare" [^2].
The human speedrun record was also set on Easy, a setting speedrunners use for exactly the same reasons [^21].
The headline claim is "to our knowledge, the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents" [^1].
That is 3h56m, with 388 tool calls across 37 distinct MCP tools and $93.17 of API-equivalent compute [^17].
The dataset card says there was "no human input after the prompt, no scripted behaviour trees, no save-scumming", and that the agent died once, to a creeper [^17].
The DeepMind paper describes it as a run on Normal difficulty with 37 high-level tools [^2].
Days later, Ronak Malde's open-source system paired a GPT-6 Astra planner with TypeSafe's JEV action model.
It killed the dragon in 8 minutes 43.3 seconds "with six bed explosions on the first landing" [^18].
It was also about 6.9 times slower and 5.6 times more expensive than the Opus run, which was given good tools [^2,17].
VPT (2022) learned from about 70,000 hours of gameplay video and became the first agent to craft diamond tools [^9].
DreamerV3 was "the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data or curricula" [^10].
Voyager unlocked tech-tree milestones "up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA" [^7], and GITM reported a +47.5% success-rate gain on ObtainDiamond [^11].
JARVIS-1 added multimodal memory and reported results on more than 200 tasks, still within the Overworld [^12].
The dragon has 200 HP and is healed by end crystals at 1 HP every half-second.
It perches, which is when it is most vulnerable, with a chance of 1 in (3 + crystals alive), so with all ten crystals standing it rarely lands [^14].
Ten crystals sit on obsidian pillars, two of them inside iron-bar cages [^15].
That is exactly the eight-hour stall the Argon team went through [^2].
The most-watched public yardstick, a Manifold market on an AI defeating the dragon before 2027, requires under 150 minutes of in-game time, human-visible observations only and random seeds.
It traded at 73% as of 2026-10-17 [^19].
METR puts it bluntly: "time horizon is not the length of time AIs can work independently" [^23].
The current record is 6:39.813, set by Skycrab on July 27, 2026 in Java 1.16.1 [^21].
Argon's run took about 245 times as long [^2,21].
Four agents running for 27h14m add up to about 109 agent-hours [^2], more than double that median.
At 20 real minutes per in-game day, the run lasted about 81.7 in-game days, which matches the paper's "about 81" [^2,40].
The team ran about 102 programs per wall-clock hour before the win [^2].
One crafting-fix helper appears in 655 programs, and a "self-stop" counter that kills leftover code from timed-out programs appears in 1,519 [^2].
One reader of Google's safety report puts Argon's internal P50 agentic time horizon at about 1.9 hours.
The paper gives about 1.35 billion input tokens, 91% served from cache, against about 16 million output tokens, of which about 4 million were thinking.
That works out to about 24,000 model calls and about $520 to the win at introductory pricing, or $1,040 at standard rates [^2].
The whole session, including the time after the win, cost about $810 ($1,620 standard) [^2].
Google made Argon generally available on October 13, 2026 at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, with cached input 95% off [^37].
The Gemini API pricing page says the introductory period ends on November 30, 2026, after which standard pricing is $4 and $20.
Divided by wall-clock time, the run cost about $19 an hour at introductory pricing [^2].
Input dominates the bill: an 84-to-1 input-to-output ratio is what happens when every call re-reads a growing context of memory, chat and program output.
ARC Prize verified Argon on ARC-AGI-3 at 49.8% with its standard harness and 97.5% with Google's "provider adapter" harness at low reasoning.
Changing only the harness roughly doubled the score, a 1.96× ratio [^24].
Epoch AI found that "simply switching the scaffold makes up to an 11% difference for GPT-5 and up to a 15% difference for Kimi K2 Thinking" on SWE-bench Verified [^27].
METR's January 2026 update to its time-horizon suite reported some models as "somewhat sensitive to scaffold (including prompting)" [^25].
Agents that "succeed on <50% of the tasks" were also "quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail)" [^28].
When Gemini 2.5 Pro finished Pokémon Blue in May 2025, the developer who built its harness said, "Please don't consider this a benchmark for how well an LLM can play Pokemon" [^32].
Before September 2026, no published agent system had reached the End at all [^7,9,10,11].
The MAST study of multi-agent LLM systems found that "performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal" and catalogued 14 failure modes [^29].
Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system beat a single agent by 90.2% on an internal evaluation.
It also found that token usage alone explained 80% of the performance variance on BrowseComp, and that most coding tasks "involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research" [^30].
The Minecraft-specific MineCollab study found agent performance "dropping as much as 15% when they are required to communicate detailed task completion plans" [^33].
A Holistic Agent Leaderboard study of 21,730 agent rollouts found that higher reasoning effort *reduced* accuracy in most runs.
For example, pearls, blaze rods and food were collected at the same time [^2].
The paper's limitations admit "the model already knows Minecraft and Mineflayer from training" [^2].
The Observer and a manual log review "found no cheating or safety incidents", but the Observer was also Gemini 4 Argon, and the review covered only a sample [^2].
Researchers who work on NetHack, a harder game, responded with deflation.
One commenter wrote that "10 year olds beat the ender dragon on a fresh world in an afternoon" and called the run "1/1000 as impressive as nethack" [^34].
Vals AI's computer-use game benchmark, which allows only keyboard and mouse, had GPT-6 Astra on top at 19.2% as of September 2026 [^20].
A skilled human kills the dragon in a minute or two.
